title: ‘The Odyssey’ Was Made for Imax 70mm. Good Luck Watching It That Way
gist: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is the first feature shot entirely on Imax film with Imax cameras, but only 41 screens worldwide (25 in the US) can project it in 15/70mm, and Imax CEO Rich Gelfond says no new film projectors have been built in about 50 years with key parts reportedly no longer in existence. Industry veteran James Hyder argues Imax has fragmented its own brand since the 2008 digital rollout — most digital Imax theaters crop to 1.90:1 on smaller screens — and that the scarcity of true Imax is commercially convenient for the company.

insights.claim: Only 41 screens worldwide — including 25 in the US — can project Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey in full Imax 70mm, while the film plays on thousands of screens in other formats, and many of the 41 are sold out for weeks.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: A hard 41-screen ceiling means premium-format demand cannot convert to revenue at scale — the constraint is physical inventory, not marketing.
insights.locator: While Nolan’s adaptation of Homer’s epic is available on thousands of screens

insights.claim: Imax CEO Rich Gelfond has said no new Imax film projectors have been made in about 50 years, so the company's strategy is retrofitting and rebuilding existing units, and Variety reported that sources at the company say many specialized parts needed to build a new one no longer exist.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The premium-format bottleneck is a decaying capital stock with no manufacturing path — Imax cannot expand its highest-margin experience even against demonstrated demand.
insights.quote: The problem is they haven’t made new Imax film projectors in about 50 years,
insights.locator: “The problem is they haven’t made new Imax film projectors

insights.claim: James Hyder disputes the parts-scarcity narrative — Imax was still building new projectors in the late 1990s and early 2000s and engineers can machine new parts — but agrees the cost and difficulty make new builds unlikely and arguably unnecessary given digital projection advances.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The constraint is economic rather than technical, which means a large enough demand signal could in principle unlock supply — but nobody expects it to.
insights.locator: In truth, Imax was still building new projectors

insights.claim: The Imax 70mm ecosystem is trapped in a chicken-and-egg loop: without projectors there are no theaters to show the film, and without films to show there is no case for the theaters.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing constraint like this only breaks with a subsidized anchor customer — which is effectively the role Nolan's films play.
insights.quote: It's the old chicken-and-egg problem. If you don't have a projector, if you don't have a theater to show it, you can't make the film.

insights.claim: Scarcity may be commercially advantageous for Imax and exhibitors rather than a problem they want solved, since rarity is itself a driver of the format's popularity.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: If constrained supply maximizes per-ticket pricing power and cultural cachet, expect no serious expansion effort regardless of demand.
insights.quote: One of the reasons this is so popular is because it's rare,
insights.locator: Of course, there are other reasons Imax and exhibitors might not mind

insights.claim: James Hyder expects existing Imax film projectors to survive for decades with good maintenance, suggesting the last one may still be running in 50 years with prints 20 to 50 years old.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The format's terminal decline is far slower than the 'no new projectors' framing implies — the installed base is the durable asset.
insights.quote: The last Imax film projector may still be running in 50 years with prints that are 20 or 50 years old,
insights.locator: That said, Hyder is still happy to see so much attention

insights.claim: The Imax film format runs an already-large 65mm negative horizontally through the camera, producing an image 15 perforations wide versus the standard 5 perf, projected at a squarish 1.43:1 aspect ratio — the technical basis for the format's sharpness and immersion.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The 15-perf horizontal spec is what cannot be replicated digitally at current resolutions — the moat and the bottleneck are the same thing.
insights.locator: For the uninitiated, the Imax film format

insights.claim: Imax now spans digital formats in 2K and 4K, xenon and laser light configurations, and classic 15/70mm, with most digital Imax theaters cropping the image to a wider 1.90:1 and projecting on screens considerably smaller than traditional giant Imax theaters.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The Imax ticket premium is charged across wildly different products — a brand-integrity risk that could eventually invite consumer or regulatory pushback.
insights.locator: Imax, though, comes in a variety of flavors

insights.claim: Imax's digital fragmentation began in 2008 with a 2K-resolution dual-projector system, a deliberate strategy to expand beyond museums and science centers into big theater chains that lacked the screen real estate a traditional Imax experience requires.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: The distribution expansion that built Imax's footprint is the direct cause of the quality dilution now undermining its premium positioning.
insights.locator: “This all started in 2008 when Imax introduced its first digital system,”

insights.claim: James Hyder, who managed the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum's Langley Imax theater and ran giant-screen trade journal LF Examiner from 2008 to 2021, argues Imax is trading on a reputation for real giant screens it no longer consistently delivers.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: An informed industry critic publicly calling the brand a disservice to customers is the kind of narrative that erodes premium pricing power over time.
insights.quote: It's a disservice to their customers, and it's basically trading on a reputation for real giant screens that used to be what Imax stood for,
insights.locator: Hyder says of the lack of clarity and consistency

insights.claim: Major theater chains investing in PLF (Premium Large Format) screens using Dolby Vision and similar systems have made it genuinely unclear whether Imax is the best available option for a given film.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: Imax faces direct competition in the premium tier from exhibitor-owned formats that keep the margin in-house — a structural threat to its licensing model.
insights.locator: Especially as major theater chains have invested in PLF

insights.claim: The Odyssey is available in six different premium formats, enough that the film's official website publishes a guide to their strengths and aspect ratios — while still failing to distinguish the wide range of experiences within 'regular' Imax.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: When a studio must ship a format explainer with its film, format proliferation has crossed from differentiation into consumer confusion.
insights.locator: Complicating things further for The Odyssey

themes.theme: Film revival and the digital replacement question

insights.claim: Imax 70mm has become the gold standard in a broader film-shooting and film-projection revival, with Dune: Part Two, Sinners, One Battle After Another and Project Hail Mary following Oppenheimer's success into Imax 70mm releases.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: A repeatable slate of premium-format tentpoles is what justifies keeping the 41-screen base alive — track which studios commit to it.
insights.locator: Recent years have seen a resurgence in shooting and projecting on film

insights.claim: The Odyssey was shot at 1.43:1 but composed so its images work when cropped all the way down to 2.39:1, deliberately engineered under Nolan's supervision to function across digital, 35mm and regular 5-perf 70mm presentations.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: Multi-format compositional discipline is what lets a premium-format film still monetize thousands of ordinary screens plus eventual Blu-ray and streaming windows.
insights.locator: While The Odyssey was shot in a 1.43:1 aspect ratio

insights.claim: A 4K laser alternative to the full 1.43:1 Imax 70mm experience exists on some old giant Imax screens but lacks the film format's sharpness; James Hyder estimates an acceptable digital replacement would require 8K projection, achievable by tiling multiple 4K projectors as planetariums routinely do.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: A concrete engineering path to replacing 15/70mm exists and is already used elsewhere — the gap is capital allocation, meaning a competitor could take it first.
insights.locator: A 4K laser alternative to the full 1.43:1 experience

insights.claim: Imax has already been supplanted by competitors on giant dome screens that formerly carried the Imax brand, according to James Hyder.
insights.speaker: Corey Atad
insights.so_what: Loss of the dome/planetarium segment is a concrete precedent for Imax losing branded installations to cheaper digital rivals.
insights.locator: noting that Imax itself has been supplanted by competitors
